questions.prompt: What is the most important interpretive limitation of ShellBags?
options: They are created by Explorer GUI browsing only, so absence proves nothing -- command-line or programmatic access generates no entry
They are deleted whenever the folder is deleted
questions.explanation: Presence is strong evidence that a path was browsed; absence is not evidence at all, since cd in a shell or a script opening a path leaves no ShellBag.

questions.prompt: Why are ShellBags valuable for paths that no longer exist?
options: They store a copy of the folder contents
The entry remains in the user's hive after the folder, drive, or share is gone -- proving a path existed and was visited
They are stored on a separate recovery partition
questions.explanation: This survivability covers deleted directories, unplugged removable media, and disconnected network shares -- often when nothing else on the system references the path.

questions.prompt: Where does the bulk of ShellBag data live on modern Windows?
questions.explanation: Because UsrClass.dat is not alongside NTUSER.DAT in the profile root, it is easy to miss -- and parsing only NTUSER.DAT gives a partial picture.

questions.prompt: Why does ShellBag attribution require care in insider threat work?
options: ShellBags never record the user account
The artifact attributes activity to an account, not a person -- an attacker in a hijacked RDP session generates ShellBags in the legitimate user's hive
ShellBags are shared across all users
questions.explanation: Since the entry lands in whichever session browsed the path, session hijacking or credential misuse produces evidence indistinguishable from the account owner's own activity.
